transcript.content: Hello, welcome in. I'm Dr. Smith. To start, can you tell me what brings you in today?

Well, Dr. Smith, I’m only here because everyone keeps saying I’ve been doing too much. My family, the neighbors... they just don't get it. To me, it feels like I’m the only one with enough drive to actually get anything done around here. 

Like, we've got this big move going on, and I'm the one getting it handled. Plus, I'm rebuilding the new garage right. You know, you can't trust these modern contractors to do a decent job. Back when I took a few engineering classes at the college—this was way before I started at the plant—they actually taught you how to measure a load-bearing beam properly. The lumber you get at the hardware store now is just awful, though. It's all warped. I spent three hours just sorting through two-by-fours yesterday to find straight ones. 

But anyway, yeah, I've got the garage, and then I’m organizing things at church because the committees there are moving slower than molasses. And on top of all that, I still have to go in and show the younger fellows at work how the job ought to be done. I run the industrial grinders and mixers, and these kids today, they just push buttons. They don't listen to the machine. I had a kid last week, Jimmy—nice boy, but a head full of rocks—he nearly burned out a motor because he wasn't paying attention to the friction pitch. I had to jump in and recalibrate the whole rig for him. 

So, I mean, they say I'm doing too much, but if I'm not doing it, who's going to?
Has this level of energy and drive to take on so many projects been a noticeable change from how you normally are, and if so, about how many days or weeks has it been going on?

Well, a change? I suppose it's a change if you look at how things were before, but it's been about a month now. Right around the time they told us we had to start clearing out of the old house. Which, let me tell you, is a whole other mess. We lived in that house for forty-two years. Forty-two years! You know how much stuff you accumulate in that time? My wife, God bless her, she never threw away a single National Geographic. We had stacks of them in the basement. I tried to tell her, "Martha, they have all this on the computer now," but she wouldn't hear of it. Said the paper felt different. And the basement, well, that's where I had my old workbench. Solid oak. They don't make them like that anymore. I had to dismantle the whole thing myself because the movers they hired—these two kids who looked like they hadn't lifted anything heavier than a video game controller—they didn't know a Phillips head from a flathead. I swear, I had to show them how to use a ratchet. But anyway, yeah, it's been about a month of me just having to handle everything.
During this past month, have you needed less sleep than usual—like only a few hours a night—while still feeling rested and full of energy?

Well, sleep? I haven't really noticed needing less of it, to be honest. I just close my eyes when the work is done, you know? But I'll tell you, getting any decent shut-eye in that new house is near impossible anyway because of the streetlights. 

They put these new LED bulbs in the lamps on our new block. The city council voted on it back in November, and I actually went to the meeting. I stood right up at the podium and told them the blue light spectrum on those things is completely wrong for a residential neighborhood. I took a physics class back in my college days, so I know a thing or two about light waves. But did the council listen? Course not. Now the street looks like a surgical ward all night. 

And don't get me started on the mattress. We had to buy a new one because those kids I mentioned, the movers, they tore the old one on a doorframe trying to pivot it down the hall. So Martha went and bought one of those memory foam things they push on TV. Terrible invention. It just traps all your body heat. You lay there sweating like you've been working the floor at the plant. When we run the big industrial grinders on a heavy load, the heat coming off the friction alone can raise the room temperature by ten degrees. You have to keep the ventilation running full blast or the particulate dust gets trapped in the air, and that's a real respiratory hazard if you aren't wearing your mask right. I'm always on the younger guys about their masks. 

But anyway, what were you asking? Oh, sleep. Yeah, I haven't really kept track of the hours.

Have you ever had a period in the past—lasting at least several days—where your mood or energy was very different from normal, either very low and depressed or unusually high and energetic, before this current month?

Well, different from normal? I don't know about that. I mean, life has its ups and downs, doesn't it? You go to work, you do your job. Like back in '98, when they had that big layoff at the plant. Now that was a stressful time. Everybody was worried about their pension. I remember sitting in the breakroom—this was before they put in those vending machines that only take exact change, which is a scam if you ask me. You put a dollar in for a sixty-five cent candy bar and it just eats the rest. Highway robbery. 

But anyway, during that layoff, I went right up to the foreman, Frank. Good guy, Frank, but he didn't know the first thing about the mixing ratios for the industrial cement we were running back then. I had to show him how the silica sand we were getting from the new supplier was too coarse. It was jamming the impellers. If you don't have the right grit, the whole batch cures too fast and you've got a solid block of concrete in a hundred-thousand-dollar machine. You have to listen to the pitch of the motor. When it starts whining like a stuck pig, you know you've got a problem. I tried explaining that to Jimmy just the other day, but kids these days, they've always got those little white things in their ears. How are you supposed to hear the machine if you're listening to a podcast or whatever they call it? 

So, I don't know. Past periods? I just keep working. That's what you do when you've got responsibilities.
Aside from stressful times at work, have you ever gone through a stretch of at least two weeks where you felt unusually sad, low on energy, or lost interest in things you normally enjoy?

Sad? Low on energy? Well, I don't know about that. I mean, sure, sometimes you get tired, but two weeks of just sitting around? Who has the time for that? Even when I retired, I didn't just stop. You can't just stop. Like my brother-in-law, Arthur. He retired from the post office back in 2012, and within six months, he was just sitting in his recliner watching daytime television. I went over there to fix a leaky P-trap under his kitchen sink—because he sure didn't know how to do it. You have to make sure the slip nuts are tight, but not too tight, or you'll crack the PVC. And you always, always use plumber's tape on the threads. But I looked at him in that chair and I said, "Arthur, you're going to turn into a piece of furniture." 

And you know what he was watching? Some game show where they bid on the price of groceries. Now, I do the shopping for me and Martha, and let me tell you, the prices they had on that show were completely out of touch with reality. A can of creamed corn for eighty-nine cents? Try a dollar fifty at the Piggly Wiggly. And the produce! Don't even get me started on the tomatoes they sell nowadays. They pick them green, gas them to turn them red, and they taste like wet cardboard. You want a real tomato, you have to grow it yourself. I used to have a beautiful garden at the old house. Big Beefsteaks, Early Girls. The trick is the soil pH. You need it right around 6.2 to 6.8. I'd mix in a little bone meal and some crushed eggshells. The calcium prevents blossom end rot. 

But, uh, no, I wouldn't say I've ever just lost interest in things. There's always something that needs doing.

Has anyone who has known you for many years—like your wife or a longtime coworker—ever told you that you went through an earlier period, even briefly, where you seemed unusually energetic, needed less sleep, or took on far more projects than usual, similar to what's happening now?

Well, people say a lot of things, don't they? Martha's always got something to say about how I do things, but energetic? I don't know about that. I just like to stay busy. You can't just sit around. Like when we were packing up the old house. I told Martha, you can't just throw everything in boxes willy-nilly. You have to have a system. I had color-coded labels for every room. Blue for the kitchen, red for the master bath. But the movers, they didn't pay a lick of attention to the labels. I watched this one kid—couldn't have been more than nineteen, wearing his pants halfway down his backside—he picked up a box marked 'Fragile: China' and just tossed it into the back of the truck like it was a sack of potatoes. 

I went right up to him and said, "Son, do you know what 'fragile' means?" He just looked at me blankly. It's the education system these days. They don't teach them basic physics. If you apply a sudden force to a brittle object, the structural integrity fails. It's the same principle we used at the plant when we were testing the tensile strength of the new polymer blends. You put it in the hydraulic press, and you watch the stress-strain curve on the monitor. If the curve dips too sharply, you've got a defective batch. I used to calibrate those presses myself. You have to use a micrometer to make sure the plates are perfectly parallel, otherwise the pressure distribution is uneven and your data is garbage. 

But, uh, what were we talking about? Oh, people saying things. Yeah, I don't really pay attention to that. I just do what needs to be done.
Have you ever been hospitalized, seen a doctor, or been prescribed any medication in the past for mood, sleep, or nerve-related problems, even briefly?

Hospitalized? For nerves or sleep? No, no, I haven't had any reason to see a doctor for anything like that. No pills or anything. I don't hold with taking a bunch of medication. 

The only time I really spent any time in a hospital was when I was in the ER back in '82. Caught my left hand in the pneumatic press at the plant. I had told the safety inspector the pressure valve was sticking, but nobody listens until somebody bleeds. You have to bleed the air lines every single week to keep the moisture out, otherwise the condensation builds up and rusts the internal cylinders. It's just basic maintenance. I used to keep a logbook, wrote down every pressure reading, every Tuesday morning at 6 AM sharp. Used a blue ballpoint pen. Has to be ballpoint, because those gel pens they sell now, they smear the second you get even a drop of machine oil on the paper. And let me tell you, there is always machine oil everywhere in a plant like that. It gets in your clothes, your hair. You can scrub your hands with Boraxo soap for an hour and you'll still smell like 10W-40. Martha used to make me leave my work boots out on the back porch because she had just put down that new linoleum in the kitchen. It had this floral pattern, very popular in the eighties, but a nightmare to keep clean if you tracked grease onto it. You have to use a solvent-based cleaner, but not too strong or it eats right through the topcoat. 

But, uh, wait, what were you asking about? Pills? No, I don't take anything for sleep or my mood. Just never needed to.
